lead: An LTI system is a system that is both linear and time-invariant. Linearity means scaling and adding inputs scales and adds the outputs. Time invariance means a delayed input gives the same output, delayed by the same amount. These two rules make a system easy to analyse: its impulse response fixes its behaviour for every input. LTI models describe audio filters, control loops, transmission lines and many sensor circuits. Indian examples include the smoothing filter in a payment app and the low-pass filter in a phone charger.
prereq: You need Unit 1: system definition, linearity, time invariance, impulse and step signals.

blocks.text: Write a continuous-time system as an operator T. Input x(t) gives output y(t)=T{x(t)}. t is time in seconds. The system is linear if the next formula holds for all inputs and constants.
T{a x₁(t) + b x₂(t)} = a T{x₁(t)} + b T{x₂(t)}
blocks.where: T is the system operator; x₁(t) and x₂(t) are any two inputs; a and b are any real constants; the output is y(t)=T{x(t)}.

blocks.text: This is superposition: scaling and adding inputs scales and adds outputs. Put a=b=0. A linear system must give T{0}=0. This zero-input test is necessary, not sufficient.

blocks.where: τ is the delay in seconds; positive τ means a delayed input; the output is delayed by the same τ.

blocks.text: Time invariance means the rule does not change with clock time. A delayed input gives the same output, delayed by τ. Some syllabi call it shift invariance. An LTI system passes both tests. LTI does not imply causal or stable; see 2.5. Continuous time only here; discrete-time LTI comes in Unit 5.
LTI matters because the impulse response h(t) and convolution follow; see 2.2 and 2.3.
Do not assume a formula is LTI because it looks simple. Use a short procedure.

items: Test linearity. Pick two easy inputs and two constants. Compute both sides of the linearity formula. One mismatch rejects the system.
Quick check: if T{0}≠0, the system is not linear.
Test time invariance. Replace t by t−τ in the input, pass through T, and compare with y(t−τ). One mismatch rejects the system.
Only systems that pass both tests are LTI.

blocks.text: A common mistake is to test with one input pair and declare linear. A pass for one choice is not proof. The formula must match for all inputs and constants. An offset such as +2 breaks linearity because T{0}=2, but it does not break time invariance. The scaling y(t)=x(2t) is time-varying: with x(t)=t and τ=1 s, delayed input x(t−1)=t−1 gives output 2t−1, while shifted output y(t−1)=2t−2. At t=1 s they give 1 and 0.

sections.h3: Why LTI is worth the trouble

blocks.text: For an LTI system, the response to an impulse δ(t) is h(t), the impulse response. Every input can be treated as a sum of shifted impulses. The output is then the convolution integral y(t)=∫x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ. This turns a system problem into one integral. In the frequency domain, an LTI system multiplies the input spectrum by a frequency response. In the Laplace domain, it gives a transfer function; see Unit 4, Laplace Transform Analysis. Non-LTI systems, such as squarers, limiters and time-scaling circuits, need other methods. Many physical systems are only approximately LTI over a small range. LTI analysis still gives the first design estimate.

figure.caption: A system must pass both tests. The example y(t)=3x(t)+2 fails the linearity test, so it is not LTI even though it passes the time-invariance test.

spec.title: LTI test
spec.aria: Flowchart tests a system for linearity first, then time invariance; a no at either test gives not LTI, and two yes gives LTI.

examples.question: Test y(t)=3x(t)+2 for linearity and time invariance. Use x₁(t)=1, x₂(t)=2, a=2, b=3 for linearity, and x(t)=t with delay τ=2 s for time invariance. Evaluate the delay test at t=5 s. State whether the system is LTI.
steps: Write the system: y(t)=3x(t)+2, so T{x}=3x+2.
Linearity test: take x₁=1, x₂=2, a=2, b=3.
Since 26 ≠ 34, the system is not linear. One counterexample is enough.
Time-invariance test: use x(t)=t and τ=2 s. Original output y(t)=3t+2.
Delayed input: x(t−2)=t−2. System output: T{x(t−2)}=3(t−2)+2=3t−4.
At t=5 s, both expressions give 3(5)−4=11. They match for all t, so the system is time-invariant.
The system is time-invariant but not linear, so it is not LTI.
examples.answer: The system is time-invariant (both sides give 11 at t = 5 s) but not linear (26 ≠ 34), so it is not an LTI system.
examples.check:
T = lambda x: 3*x + 2
lhs = T(2*1 + 3*2)
rhs = 2*T(1) + 3*T(2)
t, tau = 5, 2
out_delayed_input = 3*(t - tau) + 2
shifted_out = 3*(t - tau) + 2
print(lhs)
print(rhs)
print(out_delayed_input)
print(shifted_out)

traps: A formula with no explicit t need not be time-invariant. y(t)=x(2t) has no t in the multiplier but is time-varying.
An offset +2 breaks linearity but not time invariance. The system is time-invariant, not LTI.
T{0}=0 is necessary for linearity, not sufficient. A nonlinear system can also give zero for zero input.
One matching test does not prove linearity or time invariance. Use the full formula or compare expressions for all t.
Time-invariant does not mean the output is constant in time. It means the rule does not change with time.

quiz.q: Define an LTI system in one sentence.
quiz.a: A system that is both linear and time-invariant: it obeys superposition, and a delayed input gives the same delayed output.

quiz.q: Why must a linear system satisfy T{0}=0?
quiz.a: Set a=b=0 in T{a x₁+b x₂}=aT{x₁}+bT{x₂}. The left side is T{0}; the right side is 0.

quiz.q: Test y(t)=x(t)+3 for linearity with x₁=1, x₂=2, a=1, b=1.
quiz.a: T{1+2}=T{3}=6. T{1}+T{2}=4+5=9. Since 6 ≠ 9, the system is not linear.

quiz.q: For y(t)=x(2t), use x(t)=t, τ=1 s, t=1 s to show time variance.
quiz.a: Delayed input x(t−1)=t−1 gives output 2t−1; at t=1 s this is 1. Shifted output y(t−1)=2(t−1)=2t−2; at t=1 s this is 0. Since 1 ≠ 0, the system is time-varying.

quiz.q: A system passes time invariance but fails linearity. Is it LTI? Give the worked example.
quiz.a: No. y(t)=3x(t)+2 is time-invariant but fails linearity; LTI needs both tests to pass.

quiz.q: State two reasons LTI models are used widely.
quiz.a: The impulse response and convolution give the output; Fourier and Laplace give frequency and transfer-function views.

quiz.q: Is y(t)=2x(t)+1 linear? Is it time-invariant? Is it LTI?
quiz.a: Not linear: T{0}=1, or T{2}=5 but T{1}+T{1}=3+3=6. Time-invariant: T{x(t−τ)}=2x(t−τ)+1=y(t−τ). Not LTI.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, LTI ideas underpin audio equalisers, control loops in drones, and channel models in 5G. Real devices add saturation, drift and noise, so engineers check linearity by measurement. Researchers study linear parameter-varying and nonlinear systems when LTI is too rough. Search terms: impulse response measurement, frequency response analyser, Hammerstein model.
